title: Station flip boards are often named after a clockmaker founded in 1725

cover.alt: A large black departure board at a German railway station, with white destination names and platform numbers on rows of flaps.

body: A [split-flap display](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-flap_display) shows each character on a stack of printed flaps that flip over until the right one appears. Such boards are often called Solari boards, after **Solari di Udine**, an Italian firm founded in 1725 to make tower clocks. After the Second World War, working with designer Gino Valle, it built flip-digit time displays, then, with Belgian inventor John Myer, displays of 40 flaps that could show letters as well as numbers. In 1956 it sold its first moving sign to Liège railway station, and thousands more went to airports and stations.

slides.alt: Rows of a split-flap departure board at a German station flicker as their flaps flip over and new destinations and times appear.
slides.caption: A departure board at a German railway station: rows of flaps flip over as train destinations and times change.

left.label: Split-flap
left.text: Easy to read in most light and from wide angles, uses little or no power while still, and its clatter tells you something changed.

right.label: LED board
right.text: Changes digitally and faster, without cycling through flaps, but is harder to read.

slides.prompt: Boston's transit authority replaced the old Solari boards at North and South Station. What did it keep?
slides.detail: The new displays play a generated flapping noise to tell passengers that boarding information has changed.

slides.heading: Three centuries of Solari
slides.note: Also in 1956, Solari's Cifra 5 clock won Italy's Compasso d'Oro design award

slides.question: Why did Solari's flap displays grow from 10 flaps to 40?
slides.explanation: Its first time displays needed only the ten digits. Displays with 40 flaps, developed with John Myer, could show letters as well as numbers.
